title: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
summary: Why brute-force nearest-neighbor search stops scaling, how greedy graph search and HNSW's random layers find neighbors with a tiny fraction of the distance computations, and how to tune and choose an ANN index.
outcomes: Explain why brute-force k-NN scales linearly and why trees fail in high dimensions
Trace greedy and beam (ef) search on a proximity graph and spot a local minimum
Compute HNSW layer sizes and graph memory from M and m_L = 1/ln M
Explain how the neighbor-selection heuristic keeps clustered data connected
Tune M, ef_construction and ef against recall@k, and pick HNSW, IVF or PQ for a constraint

lessons.title: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you turned text into embeddings and ranked documents by cosine similarity to a query embedding. That ranking is a **k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) search**: given a query vector $q$ and $N$ stored vectors, return the $k$ vectors closest to $q$ under some distance (Euclidean, inner product or cosine).

The obvious way is **brute force**: compute the distance from $q$ to every stored vector and keep the best $k$. It is exact and simple. Its cost is the problem: every query touches every vector, so the work grows linearly with $N$.

blocks.tex: \text{cost per query} = N \times d \ \text{multiply-adds}, \qquad \text{bytes read} = N \times d \times 4 \ (\text{float32})
blocks.caption: Brute force reads every stored vector once per query.

blocks.md: Put in real sizes. Ten million documents embedded in 768 dimensions is $10^7 \times 768 = 7.68 \times 10^9$ multiply-adds per query, and $7.68 \times 10^9 \times 4$ bytes = **30.72 GB** of float32 data to stream through the CPU. Under a simple model where the scan is limited by a memory bandwidth of 100 GB/s, that is about 0.31 seconds for one query, before you serve a second user.

blocks.title: Brute-force latency grows linearly with collection size

scenes.caption: Simplified model: latency = N x d x 4 bytes / bandwidth. At 768 dimensions and 100 GB/s, 10 million vectors take about 307 ms per query, far over a 10 ms budget.
Ten times more bandwidth (1000 GB/s) only shifts the line down by 10x. The slope stays 1: double the data, double the time. Hardware cannot fix a linear scan.
Smaller vectors (128 dimensions) help by a constant factor too, but the line is still linear in N. We need an algorithm that looks at a tiny fraction of the vectors.

blocks.md: Classic exact indexes such as k-d trees speed this up only in low dimensions. The HNSW paper puts it plainly: exact k-NN methods offer substantial speedups only for relatively low-dimensional data, because of the **curse of dimensionality**. One symptom is easy to measure: in high dimensions, the nearest and farthest points end up at almost the same distance, so pruning rules like "this whole region is too far away" rarely fire.

blocks.prompt: Draw 1000 random Gaussian points and one random query. In 2 dimensions the farthest point is about 100 times farther than the nearest. What do you expect that ratio to be in 768 dimensions?
blocks.reveal: About **1.16**. We computed it (20 trials of 1000 points each): the ratio is 103 in 2-d, 2.9 in 16-d, 1.44 in 128-d and 1.16 in 768-d. When every point is almost equally far, a tree cannot discard whole branches, so it degrades toward visiting everything.

blocks.title: Farthest over nearest distance, random Gaussian data

scenes.caption: Mean ratio of farthest to nearest distance from a random query to 1000 random Gaussian points (20 trials, computed with a script). In 2-d the contrast is huge.

Zoom on the high-dimensional cases: by 768-d the farthest point is only 16 percent farther than the nearest. Distance-based pruning has almost nothing to work with. (Real embeddings are less uniform than this, which is why ANN still works well on them.)

blocks.md: So practical systems give up on exactness. **Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)** search allows a few mistakes in exchange for touching a tiny fraction of the data. Quality is measured by **recall@k**: the fraction of the true $k$ nearest neighbors (found by brute force) that the index returned. If the true top 5 is {3, 9, 14, 22, 40} and the index returns {3, 9, 14, 40, 51}, recall@5 is 4/5 = 0.8.

scenes.caption: Brute force gives the ground truth: the ids of the 5 vectors truly closest to the query, in order.
The ANN index returns 5 ids. Four of them (3, 9, 14, 40) are in the true top 5.
Id 22 was missed and id 51 slipped in. Recall@5 = 4/5 = 0.8. Order inside the top k does not matter for this metric.

blocks.md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

Cosine similarity and inner product are not the same metric. If your embeddings are not unit-length, an inner-product index ranks differently from cosine. Faiss documents the standard fix: normalize vectors to length 1, then inner product equals cosine similarity.

blocks.question: Your collection grows from 1 million to 4 million vectors and you upgrade to a machine with 2x the memory bandwidth. Under the linear-scan model, what happens to brute-force latency?
options: It stays the same, because the bandwidth doubled
It doubles: 4x the data over 2x the bandwidth
It quadruples, because bandwidth does not affect latency
It halves, because more bandwidth beats more data
blocks.explain: Brute force reads every vector, so time scales with N divided by bandwidth: 4 / 2 = 2x slower. Hardware gives constant factors; the linear growth in N remains.

blocks.question: An index returns 10 results for a query; 7 of them are among the true 10 nearest neighbors. A colleague says recall@10 is 0.7, but because the 7 are ranked in a different order than the exact ones, the real recall is lower. Who is right?
options: The colleague: order mismatches reduce recall@10
You: recall@10 counts overlap with the true top 10, so it is 0.7
Neither: recall needs the distances, not the ids
The colleague: recall@10 is only defined for exact order
blocks.explain: Recall@k, as defined in the HNSW paper, is the number of true nearest neighbors found divided by k. It is a set overlap; ranking quality inside the top k is a separate metric.

lessons.title: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters

blocks.md: A different idea: instead of partitioning space, connect each stored vector to a few of its near neighbors, forming a **proximity graph**. To search, start at some entry node and repeatedly hop to whichever neighbor is closer to the query. Each hop needs only a handful of distance computations, so if the path is short, the search is cheap.

This is the **Navigable Small World (NSW)** idea that HNSW builds on. A graph is *navigable* if greedy routing finds its target in a small (logarithmic or polylogarithmic) number of hops. The HNSW paper notes the ideal graph for this is the Delaunay graph, where greedy search always ends at the true nearest neighbor, but it cannot be built efficiently in high dimensions, so practical methods approximate it with near-neighbor links.

Here is a tiny hand-built graph of 8 points on a 2-d grid, with node A as the entry point. The query sits at grid position (5, 5). Each node's badge shows its Euclidean distance to the query, computed from grid coordinates. The true nearest neighbor is **H** at distance 1.41.

blocks.prompt: Greedy search starts at A and always moves to the neighbor closest to the query, stopping when no neighbor is closer than the current node. Trace it on the figure's first scene. Which node does it return?
blocks.reveal: It returns **F** (distance 2.0), not H (1.41). The path is A, C, D, F. At F, both neighbors (D at 2.83, E at 5.0) are farther from the query, so greedy stops. F is a **local minimum**: better than all its neighbors, but not the global best. The edge to H hangs off G, which greedy passed over because F looked better at D.

blocks.title: Greedy search gets stuck; a wider beam escapes

scenes.caption: Toy graph (hand-built, 8 nodes). Badges show each node's distance to the query. Entry point A is far away (7.07). The true nearest neighbor is H (1.41).
Greedy, step 1: at A, compute distances to neighbors B (5.0) and C (4.47). C is closest to the query, so hop to C.
Step 2: C's new neighbors are D (2.83) and E (5.0). Hop to D. Each hop costs only one distance per new neighbor.
Step 3: at D, neighbors F (2.0) and G (3.0) are new. F is closest, so greedy hops to F and forgets G.
Step 4: F's neighbors D (2.83) and E (5.0) are both farther than F (2.0). Greedy stops and returns F. It never saw H: a local minimum after 7 distance evaluations.
Beam search with ef = 3 keeps the 3 best nodes found so far, not just 1. After expanding D the list is F (2.0), D (2.83), G (3.0), so G stays in play.
Expanding F adds nothing new, so the search expands G next and discovers H (1.41). The final list is H, F, D: the true nearest neighbor is found, at the cost of one more distance (8 in total).

blocks.md: The fix shown in the last two scenes is the search procedure HNSW actually uses (Algorithm 2, SEARCH-LAYER, in the paper). It keeps two sets: **C**, the candidates still to expand, ordered nearest first, and **W**, the best $ef$ nodes found so far. It repeatedly expands the nearest candidate and stops when the nearest remaining candidate is farther than the worst member of W, because nothing reachable through it can improve W.

blocks.title: SEARCH-LAYER on the toy graph with ef = 3

scenes.caption: Start at entry point A (7.07). Both lists hold just A.
Expand A. W has room (fewer than 3), so B (5.0) and C (4.47) are added to both lists.
Expand C. D (2.83) beats the worst of W and enters; A is evicted. E (5.0) is not strictly better than B (5.0), so it is skipped.
Expand D. F (2.0) and G (3.0) both beat the worst of W, pushing out B and C. With ef = 1, G would have been dropped here.
Expand F. Its neighbors D and E were already visited, so nothing changes.
Expand G. H (1.41) is new and better than the worst member (G 3.0), so H enters and G leaves W.
Expand H: no new neighbors. Next candidate is B at 5.0, farther than W's worst (D 2.83), so the loop breaks and returns W.

blocks.md: $ef$ is the size of the result list W. A larger $ef$ explores more of the graph, escapes more local minima and raises recall, at the cost of more distance computations. To return $k$ results you need $ef \ge k$; hnswlib documents that ef cannot be set lower than k.

Greedy graph search has no guarantee of exactness on a real (non-Delaunay) graph. Even a large $ef$ can miss a neighbor if the graph has no path that improves toward it. Recall comes from how well the graph is built, which is the subject of the next two lessons.

blocks.question: In SEARCH-LAYER, why is it safe to stop when the nearest remaining candidate is farther than the worst element of W?
options: Because the graph is guaranteed to be a Delaunay graph
Because all ef results have already been found exactly
Because every remaining candidate is farther than all ef results, and the search assumes their neighbors are unlikely to be closer; it is a heuristic stop, not a proof
Because distances in high dimensions are all equal
blocks.explain: Candidates farther than W's worst cannot enter W, and the search assumes their neighbors are unlikely to be better. That is the approximation: on a well-built graph it rarely loses true neighbors, but it is not an exactness guarantee.

blocks.question: On the toy graph, greedy search (ef = 1) returned F instead of H. Which change would most directly let it find H?
options: Start from F instead of A
Raise ef so G is kept in the result list
Use cosine distance instead of Euclidean
Remove the edge between D and F
blocks.explain: With ef = 3, G (3.0) survives in W after D is expanded, and expanding G reveals H. Changing the start node or edges is not something you control per query; ef is the query-time knob.

lessons.title: HNSW layers: a skip list made of graphs

blocks.md: A flat NSW graph has a scaling problem. The HNSW paper explains that greedy routing in NSW has polylogarithmic complexity: the number of hops grows with $\log N$, and the number of links checked at each hub also grows with $\log N$. Search starts with many short hops before it reaches the region of the query.

HNSW fixes this the way a **skip list** speeds up a sorted linked list. A skip list keeps the full list at the bottom, plus sparser "express" lists above it that skip many elements per step. HNSW does the same with graphs: layer 0 holds every vector; each higher layer holds a random, exponentially smaller subset, so its links span longer distances. Search starts at the top, takes a few long hops, then drops a layer and refines.
Each vector's top layer is chosen at random when it is inserted (line 4 of the paper's Algorithm 1):

blocks.caption: A vector with level l is present in layers 0 through l. The paper recommends this m_L, and hnswlib sets mult_ = 1 / log(M).

blocks.md: With $m_L = 1/\ln M$, the probability that a vector reaches layer $\ell$ or higher is $M^{-\ell}$. The paper notes this matches a skip list with $p = 1/M$, which gives each layer about $1/M$ as many nodes as the one below. Here $M$ is also the number of links each new node creates per layer, so one parameter sets both the fan-out and the layer shrink rate.

blocks.title: Sampling levels for 10 inserts with M = 4

scenes.caption: Ten uniform random draws (seeded script). With M = 4, mL = 1/ln 4 = 0.721.
Transform each draw: -ln(u) x 0.721. Small u gives a large value; this produces an exponential distribution.
Floor gives the level. Six of ten land on layer 0 only. Four reach layer 1 or higher (expected 10 x 1/4 = 2.5).

Element 6 drew level 3, the highest so far, so it becomes the entry point: every search starts at its top layer. If a later insert draws a higher level, it takes over (lines 18 and 19 of Algorithm 1).

blocks.title: Expected nodes per layer: 1 million vectors, M = 16

scenes.caption: Layer 0 holds all 1,000,000 vectors. On a linear axis everything else is invisible: the upper layers are tiny.
Without layer 0: N x 16^-l gives 62,500 nodes on layer 1, 3,906 on layer 2, 244 on layer 3, 15 on layer 4 and about 1 on layer 5. The top layer is near log base 16 of 10^6 = 4.98.

blocks.md: Search (Algorithm 5 in the paper) uses this structure in two phases. On every layer above 0 it runs SEARCH-LAYER with $ef = 1$, a plain greedy descent, and uses the node it ends on as the entry point for the next layer down. On layer 0 it runs SEARCH-LAYER with the user's $ef$ and returns the best $k$ of the result list.

blocks.title: Descending the layers on the toy graph

scenes.caption: Simplified: we assign levels by hand (A and G at level 2, H at level 1, the rest at 0). Layer 2 holds only A and G, linked by one long edge. Search starts at the entry point A.
Greedy on layer 2: G (3.0) is closer than A (7.07), so hop to G. G has no closer neighbor here, so G becomes the entry point for layer 1. One long hop crossed most of the space.
Layer 1 holds A, G and H. From G, neighbor H (1.41) is closer, so hop to H. H has no closer neighbor on this layer.
Layer 0 has every node. Starting from H, even plain greedy (ef = 1) cannot improve: H is the answer. Flat greedy from A ended at F; starting near the target avoids that local minimum.

blocks.md: The hierarchy also has a modest memory cost. Each node stores up to $M_{max0}$ links on layer 0 and up to $M_{max}$ on each upper layer it belongs to. The paper approximates the average number of upper layers per node by $m_L$ (the exact value with the floor is $1/(M-1)$, about 0.067 for $M = 16$, so this slightly overestimates), and gives the average graph memory per vector as:

blocks.caption: With 4-byte link ids, M_max = M and M_max0 = 2M. The paper reports 60 to 450 bytes per object for M from 6 to 48.

blocks.md: Compare that with the vector itself: 768 float32 dimensions are 3,072 bytes, so the graph adds about 5 percent. For HNSW the dominant memory cost is usually the raw vectors, which must stay in RAM because every hop computes exact distances against them.

blocks.question: With M = 16 and the recommended m_L, roughly what fraction of vectors appear on layer 2 or above?
options: 1/16, about 6 percent
1/32, about 3 percent
1/256, about 0.4 percent
1/2, because each layer halves
blocks.explain: P(level at least l) = M^-l, so layer 2 or above has probability 16^-2 = 1/256. Layer 1 or above is 1/16. The shrink factor per layer is M, not 2.

blocks.question: A teammate sets m_L very high (for example 5) so the hierarchy is taller. What does the HNSW paper say happens when m_L is too large?
options: Neighbors overlap more across layers, so extra layers add little and search gets slower
Recall drops to zero because layer 0 becomes empty
Memory shrinks because fewer links are stored
Nothing changes; m_L only affects build time
blocks.explain: The paper explains that larger m_L means more overlap between layers (more nodes repeated on many layers), which hurts performance, while too small m_L increases the number of hops on each layer. That tradeoff is why it picks m_L = 1/ln M, matching a skip list with p = 1/M.

lessons.title: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic

blocks.md: HNSW is built by inserting vectors one at a time (Algorithm 1 in the paper). Inserting vector $q$ looks a lot like searching for it:

1. Draw $q$'s level $\ell$ with the formula from the last lesson.
2. From the entry point, descend greedily ($ef = 1$) through the layers above $\ell$.
3. On each layer from $\min(L, \ell)$ down to 0, run SEARCH-LAYER with $ef = ef_{construction}$ to collect candidates, pick $M$ of them as $q$'s neighbors, and add links in **both** directions.
4. If a neighbor now has more than $M_{max}$ links ($M_{max0}$ on layer 0), shrink its list with the same selection rule.
5. If $\ell$ is above the current top layer, $q$ becomes the new entry point.

Step 3 hides the key design choice: *which* $M$ candidates become neighbors. The simple rule (Algorithm 3) takes the $M$ closest. The paper's **heuristic** (Algorithm 4) walks candidates from nearest to farthest and keeps candidate $e$ only if $e$ is closer to $q$ than to every neighbor already kept. A candidate that is closer to a kept neighbor is skipped, because $q$ can already reach it through that neighbor.

blocks.tex: \text{keep } e \iff \operatorname{dist}(e, q) < \operatorname{dist}(e, r) \ \text{ for every already-kept } r \in R
blocks.caption: Paper Algorithm 4, line 11. hnswlib's getNeighborsByHeuristic2 implements the same test.

blocks.prompt: New node q has two clusters of candidates: e1, e2, e3 close by on its left (distances 1.0, 2.0, 1.41) and e4, e5 farther away on its right (3.0, 3.16). With M = 2, which two neighbors does each rule pick?
blocks.reveal: The **simple rule** picks e1 and e3, the two closest, both in the left cluster. The **heuristic** keeps e1, rejects e3 (it is 1.0 from e1 but 1.41 from q) and e2 (1.0 from e1, 2.0 from q), then keeps e4 (4.0 from e1, only 3.0 from q). Result: e1 and e4, one link into each cluster.

blocks.title: Neighbor selection: simple rule vs heuristic (M = 2)

scenes.caption: Candidates found by SEARCH-LAYER for new node q, with distances to q (grid coordinates, computed). The left cluster is close; the right cluster is reachable only through q's links.
Simple rule: keep the 2 closest, e1 (1.0) and e3 (1.41). Both are in the left cluster. Nothing links q toward the right cluster.
Heuristic, nearest first: e1 (1.0) is kept automatically because R is empty.
e3: distance to e1 is 1.0, less than its distance to q (1.41). q can already reach e3 through e1, so e3 is skipped. e2 fails the same way (1.0 to e1 vs 2.0 to q).
e4: distance to e1 is 4.0, more than its 3.0 to q, so it is kept. R is now full (M = 2). The heuristic chose one link per direction, a bridge between clusters.

blocks.md: Why does that matter? On clustered data, the simple rule links each new node only into its own cluster, and clusters can end up disconnected: no greedy path leads from one to another. The paper says the heuristic helps most on clustered data and makes little difference on uniform, very high-dimensional data. We checked this with a small pure-Python implementation of the paper's algorithms.

blocks.title: Recall@10: simple rule vs heuristic (our experiment)

scenes.caption: Setup: 20,000 vectors in 16-d, M = 8, M_max0 = 16, ef_construction = 64, 200 queries, recall@10 vs brute force. Uniform = one Gaussian; clustered = 50 Gaussian clusters. At ef = 64:

Doubling ef to 128 helps the uniform graphs, but the simple rule on clustered data barely moves (79.9 percent): the missing neighbors sit in clusters that greedy search cannot reach. More search effort cannot fix missing links.

blocks.md:
The construction parameters, as documented in the paper and hnswlib:

- **M**: links created per new node per layer. The paper suggests 5 to 48; hnswlib says 12 to 48 suits most uses, with higher M for high intrinsic dimensionality or high recall. Memory grows linearly in M.
- **M_max0 = 2M** on layer 0. The paper found $M_{max0} = M$ causes a strong penalty at high recall, and values above 2M waste memory without speedup.
- **ef_construction**: the beam width while inserting. It should be large enough that construction-time search reaches recall near 1 (the paper says 0.95 is enough for most uses); beyond that, raising it only slows the build.
hnswlib's check for a good ef_construction: build the index, set ef = ef_construction, and measure recall for an M-nearest-neighbor search. If recall is below 0.9, there is room to improve the graph.

Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; lesson 5 shows how libraries handle them.

blocks.question: You build HNSW over product embeddings grouped into tight categories, using the simple closest-M rule. Recall plateaus near 80 percent no matter how high you set ef. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: ef is still too low; raise it to 10,000
The categories are disconnected in the graph; use the diversity heuristic when selecting neighbors
M_max0 is too large; set it equal to M
The level formula is wrong; set m_L to 0
blocks.explain: A plateau that ef cannot lift means the graph lacks paths, not search effort. The heuristic keeps links that point in diverse directions, including bridges between clusters, which is exactly the case the paper's Figure 2 illustrates.

blocks.question: Which change increases index build time but leaves query-time cost per ef roughly the same?
options: Raising ef at query time
Raising ef_construction
Raising M
Raising the dimension d
blocks.explain: ef_construction only controls the beam width during inserts. M also raises query cost because every expanded node has more neighbors to score; d makes every distance more expensive; ef is the query knob itself.

lessons.title: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ

blocks.md: In production you tune one knob at query time and two at build time. The query-time knob is **ef** (`set_ef` in hnswlib, `efSearch` in Faiss, `hnsw.ef_search` in pgvector). Each value of ef gives one point on a recall versus speed curve, and you pick the cheapest point that meets your recall target. ANN-Benchmarks evaluates libraries exactly this way: sweep parameters, then plot quality against speed.

blocks.title: Sweeping ef: recall vs work (our experiment)

scenes.caption: Recall@10 on 20,000 uniform 16-d vectors (M = 8, ef_construction = 64, 200 queries). Recall rises quickly then saturates: 56.8, 69.4, 85.2, 95.1, 98.9 percent.
Distance computations per query as a percent of brute force (20,000): 1.0, 1.3, 2.1, 3.5, 6.0 percent. Going from 95.1 to 98.9 percent recall costs 1.7x more work.

blocks.md:
HNSW is not the only ANN family. The two you will meet most often, both documented in Faiss:

- **IVF (inverted file)**: k-means clusters the vectors into `nlist` cells. A query scans only the `nprobe` cells whose centroids are closest, roughly a fraction nprobe/nlist of the data. It fails when the true neighbor's cell is not probed. pgvector suggests starting with lists = rows/1000 (up to 1M rows) and probes = sqrt(lists).
- **PQ (product quantization)**: splits each vector into $m$ sub-vectors and replaces each with an 8-bit codebook id, so a vector costs about $m$ bytes, and distances are estimated from the codes. It saves memory at some accuracy cost and is often combined with IVF (Faiss `IndexIVFPQ`).

blocks.title: Bytes per 768-d vector by index type

scenes.caption: From the Faiss index table: Flat stores 4d = 3,072 bytes. IVF,Flat adds an 8-byte id (3,080). For HNSW we add the paper's average graph cost of about 151 bytes (3,223).

Compression changes the picture: 8-bit scalar quantization stores d + 8 = 776 bytes; PQ with 96 one-byte codes stores 96 + 8 = 104 bytes. At 10 million vectors that is about 1 GB instead of 30.7 GB for the raw floats.

blocks.md: Rules of thumb that follow from the mechanisms: HNSW gives strong recall versus speed, supports incremental inserts without training, but needs the full vectors and graph in RAM. IVF needs a training pass (k-means) and has a cheaper build and smaller overhead; pgvector's docs describe IVFFlat as faster to build and smaller than HNSW but with a worse speed versus recall tradeoff. PQ is what you add when memory, not speed, is the binding constraint. Faiss can also combine them, for example HNSW over compressed codes (`IndexHNSWSQ`, `IndexHNSWPQ`).

blocks.caption: pgvector's HNSW index; m = 16 and ef_construction = 64 are the defaults its README lists, and <=> is cosine distance.

blocks.prompt: You add `WHERE category = 'shoes'` to that query. Shoes are 10 percent of the table, and hnsw.ef_search is 40. How many rows do you expect back from LIMIT 10?
blocks.reveal: About **4**, not 10. pgvector applies the filter *after* the index scan: the scan produces ef_search = 40 candidates, and on average 10 percent of them (4) match. pgvector's README gives exactly this example. The fixes are raising ef_search, enabling iterative index scans (`hnsw.iterative_scan`, which keeps scanning until enough rows match), or using a partial index or partitioning for very selective filters.

blocks.md: Filtered vector search is the most common production surprise. Post-filtering an ANN result can return fewer than k rows and silently lower recall. Check whether your engine pre-filters, post-filters or scans iteratively. hnswlib, for example, accepts a filter in knn_query that restricts results to allowed ids.

Two more operational facts. **Deletes**: Faiss documents that its HNSW index does not support removing vectors; hnswlib offers `mark_deleted`, which hides an element from results while keeping it in the graph for routing, and can later reuse the slot with `replace_deleted`. **Builds**: insertion cost scales like search, so the paper reports roughly $O(N \log N)$ construction for low-dimensional data, and hnswlib parallelizes `add_items` across threads.

blocks.code:
import hnswlib
import numpy as np

dim, n = 768, 10000
data = np.random.rand(n, dim).astype('float32')

index = hnswlib.Index(space='cosine', dim=dim)
index.init_index(max_elements=n, M=16, ef_construction=200)
index.add_items(data, np.arange(n))

index.set_ef(64)  # query-time beam width; must be >= k
labels, distances = index.knn_query(data[:5], k=10)
blocks.caption: hnswlib's Python API, following its README. Measure recall against brute force before trusting any setting.

blocks.md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

blocks.question: Your HNSW service hits 99 percent recall@10 but p99 latency is too high. Memory is fine and you cannot rebuild today. What is the right first move?
options: Lower M
Lower ef and re-measure recall vs latency
Lower ef_construction
Switch the metric from cosine to L2
blocks.explain: ef is the only knob that applies without a rebuild; M and ef_construction are fixed at build time. Our sweep shows recall saturates near the top, so a modest drop in ef can cut work substantially for a small recall loss.

blocks.question: You must index 1 billion 768-d vectors on machines with limited RAM. Which choice best fits the constraint?
options: HNSW,Flat, because it has the best recall versus speed
Brute force on GPUs, because it is exact
IVF with PQ codes, because each vector shrinks from 3,072 bytes to around 100
HNSW with a larger M, because more links mean less memory
blocks.explain: Raw float32 vectors alone would be about 3 TB, and HNSW,Flat needs them in RAM. IVF,PQ stores about m + 8 bytes per vector (about 104 GB with 96 codes), at some accuracy cost. A larger M increases memory, it does not reduce it.

blocks.question: A query with a selective filter (1 percent of rows match) returns 0 or 1 results from an HNSW index with ef_search = 40. Which explanation fits?
options: The graph is disconnected, so the filtered rows are unreachable
The index post-filters about 40 candidates, so about 0.4 match on average
Cosine distance cannot be combined with WHERE clauses
ef_search is ignored when a filter is present
blocks.explain: With post-filtering, expected matches = candidates times selectivity = 40 x 0.01 = 0.4. Raise ef_search, enable iterative scans, or use a separate index or partition for that filter.

sources.label: Malkov and Yashunin, Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using HNSW graphs
